newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries down at midday, weakened by data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries down at midday, weakened by data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices were down at midday on Thursday, partly due to some stronger than expected economic data, analysts said.
The 6-1/2 percent 30-year bond, already down 6/32 or 7/32 before any data were released, was down 9/32 to 100-10/32, yielding 6.60 percent, at midday.
The market got three economic reports -- January housing starts data, weekly jobless claims, and the February Philadelphia Federal Reserve survey. The first two of these mainly offset one another.
The government reported that housing starts rose 2.0 percent to an annualized rate of 1.350 million in January from a revised annualized rate of 1.323 million in December.
While this constituted a bounce, economists had anticipated a stronger head of steam, looking for a level of new starts closer to 1.42 million for January.

But new claims for jobless benefits in the latest week were a fewer than expected 309,000 after a revised 308,000 new claims a week earlier. Economists had expected claims to climb to more than 320,000, a level they said would easily be consistent with average payroll growth of 200,00 jobs per month.

"The data were a mixed bag," said Josh Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "The jobless claims were at pretty low levels -- very low levels. It seems pretty clear that the labor market is still quite strong and that the economy is generating a lot of new jobs."
The market approached the mid-morning release of the Philadelphia Federal Reserve Bank survey at levels little changed from early dealings.
The lows of the day were reached after the February survey of business conditions in the Philadelphia area came in stronger than expected.
The 6-1/2 percent 30-year long bond dipped a little over a quarter of a point after the Philadelphia Fed survey, but erased even that loss in subsequent trading.
At midday, prices reapproached session lows.
"The market's pretty quiet," said Matthew Alexy, chief markets strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston. "It's wandering around looking for direction."

Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc., took note of the market's downward drift over the last couple of sessions, despite a friendly January Consumer Price Index (CPI) on Wednesday and Thursday's housing data.
"That suggests that 6-1/2 percent on the long bond yield is about as low as we can go," he said. "We would need new incentives to go lower."
Analysts said the market now has turned its eye toward Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before the Senate on February 26.
"Humphrey-Hawkins is clearly a benchmark event for the market," said Alexy. "We could see some pretty boring activity until we see the Humphrey-Hawkins (testimony)," he said.
In early afternoon dealings, three- and six-month bill rates were unchanged at 4.96 percent and 5.03 percent, respectively.
Two-year notes were down 1/32 to 100-3/32, yielding 5.82 percent. Five-year notes were down 3/32 at 100-16/32, yielding 6.13 percent. Ten-year notes were down 6/32 at 99-11/32, yielding 6.34 percent.
